To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

prostate cancer screening has not been shown to improve survival, that screening can lead to overtreatment, that screening is expensive and may cause harm, that the benefits of screening are unclear, that the benefits are likely to be small, and that the harms of screening are large.
the PSA test is a good screening test for prostate cancer.
the use of PSA screening in men aged 55 to 69 is associated with a reduction in the risk of death from prostate cancer of 20%.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: 1) the natural history of prostate cancer and the role of screening in its management, 2) the strengths and weaknesses associated with the use of PSA and other screening methodologies, and 3) the epidemiologic considerations of screening in the management of prostate cancer.
understanding the natural history and epidemiology of prostate cancer and with the development and validation of new screening methodologies for early detection of this disease.
the development of new technologies for prostate cancer screening, and the evaluation of the clinical use of prostate cancer screening.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
prostate cancer screening is not yet ready for prime time.
the use of screening for early detection of prostate cancer is premature.
the evidence does not yet support the widespread use of screening for prostate cancer in the general male population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the natural history of prostate cancer is not completely known, the strengths and weakness of available screening methodologies are not well understood, and the risk of prostate cancer in different populations is not well defined.
screening for prostate cancer has been shown to detect a high number of cases, but has not been shown to reduce mortality from prostate cancer.

the current evidence supports the use of prostate cancer screening in the form of a digital rectal examination (DRE) and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) in men older than 50 years of age who have a life expectancy of at least 10 years and who understand the limitations of the test and the need for a follow-up biopsy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current evidence does not support routine screening for prostate cancer.
we should not be screening for prostate cancer.

we need to continue to work to understand the natural history of prostate cancer, and to develop and validate biomarkers that can improve the detection of aggressive disease and the prevention of unnecessary treatment of indolent disease.
